name: NVIDIA
summary: NVIDIA's hiring page describes phone interviews followed by virtual or in-person interviews with the hiring manager, team members and people from other groups, and says technical candidates may be asked to complete a coding exercise. Candidates commonly report deep technical interviews in their own area: GPU and computer architecture, chip design and verification, systems software, parallel programming or deep learning. NVIDIA publishes five core values, including Intellectual Honesty and Speed & Agility.
rounds: Online application; NVIDIA suggests applying to the few roles that best match your background
Phone interviews with a recruiter, the hiring manager or engineers
Coding exercise for some technical roles, often on HackerRank
Virtual or in-person interviews: one-on-one, small-group or panel, usually 30–60 minutes each
NVIDIA's hiring page says an in-person interview at an office is needed before an offer; interns typically have phone interviews only
looks_for: Intellectual Honesty: seek truth, learn from mistakes, share learnings
One Team: do what's best for the company
Deep knowledge of your area, from computer architecture to deep learning
Clear reasoning out loud on technical problems
Projects that show you've applied your skills, not only studied them

questions.text: Tell me about a mistake you made and how you shared what you learned with your team.
covers: The mistake, stated plainly and without excuses
How you fixed it
How you shared the lesson so others wouldn't repeat it

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to change direction quickly because the situation changed.
covers: What changed and how you noticed
How quickly you adjusted the plan and brought others along
The result, and what would have happened if you hadn't changed

questions.text: Tell me about a time you kept going on a hard technical problem when an easy workaround was available.
covers: The problem and the tempting shortcut
Why the proper fix was worth the extra effort
How you solved it and what it made possible

questions.text: Tell me about a time you put the wider company's goal ahead of your own team's plan.
covers: The conflict between the two goals
How you decided and who you involved
The outcome for the company and for your team

questions.text: Explain how a GPU differs from a CPU, and which kinds of work suit each.
covers: Few powerful cores tuned for low latency versus many simpler cores tuned for throughput
Memory bandwidth and the cost of moving data between host and device
Examples: branchy serial code on the CPU, data-parallel maths on the GPU

questions.text: What is a GPU kernel in CUDA terms, and what usually limits its performance?
covers: Threads, blocks and warps, and how work maps onto them
Memory access patterns such as coalescing, plus shared memory use
Occupancy and branch divergence, and how a profiler shows the limit

questions.text: How would you speed up matrix multiplication on a GPU? Talk me through the ideas rather than the code.
covers: Tiling so blocks reuse data from shared memory
Coalesced loads, and using specialised matrix hardware and lower precision where accuracy allows
Measuring against the hardware's peak to know how much is left

questions.text: What is a race condition, how would you find one, and how would you prevent it in parallel code?
covers: Two threads accessing shared data, at least one writing, without ordering
Finding it with careful review, stress tests and race-detection tools
Prevention: atomics, locks, barriers, or designs that avoid shared writes

questions.text: How would you verify a hardware block such as an arbiter or cache controller? What would your test plan cover?
covers: Features and corner cases: fairness, back-pressure, simultaneous requests, reset
Random stimulus with a reference model, plus assertions
Coverage goals and how you'd decide verification is complete

questions.text: Training a model across many GPUs is slower than expected. How would you find the bottleneck?
covers: Checking GPU utilisation first: are the GPUs waiting on data loading?
Communication cost between GPUs, batch size and how it scales
Profiling one step end to end, then fixing the biggest gap

questions.text: Explain the trade-offs of running a neural network at lower precision, such as FP16 or INT8.
covers: Gains: speed, memory and power
Risks: accuracy loss, overflow and underflow
Mitigations such as mixed precision, scaling and calibration, with accuracy checks

questions.text: How would you debug a graphics driver crash that only happens in one game?
covers: Reproducing it and collecting crash dumps and driver logs
Comparing driver versions, GPUs and settings to narrow it down
Capturing the frame or API calls that trigger it, then fixing and adding a regression test

questions.text: Why NVIDIA, and which of its platforms or products would you most like to work on?
covers: A specific platform, product or research area
A link to your own projects or studies
What you'd want to build or learn there

questions.text: What recent development in GPUs, AI or graphics excites you, and why?
covers: One development, explained simply and accurately
Why it matters technically or for users
How it connects to the work you want to do

tips: Know the fundamentals for your track deeply: computer architecture and parallel programming for GPU roles, digital design and verification for hardware, linear algebra and deep learning for AI.
NVIDIA's hiring page recommends applying to the top three to five roles that match your background rather than many.
NVIDIA's hiring page warns that using unapproved outside tools during an interview leads to disqualification.
For a coding exercise, practise writing tested, readable code in a browser-based editor under time limits.
Prepare one project in depth with its numbers: speed-ups, utilisation, accuracy, area or power.
